findings.title: Dead code: two ASN1Encoder instances created and immediately discarded
findings.body: Lines 114-115 create two `ASN1Encoder` instances, call `.write()` on them, and discard the results. The actual encoding is correctly performed on lines 117-121. These two lines are dead code (likely leftover from development) that allocate objects for no purpose. They should be removed to avoid confusion.

findings.title: New abstract method `order()` added to public interface breaks existing implementations
findings.body: Adding `int order()` as a non-default method to the `CryptoProvider` interface is a source-incompatible change. Any third-party or extension module that implements `CryptoProvider` will fail to compile after upgrading. Consider providing a default implementation (e.g., `default int order() { return 0; }`) to preserve backward compatibility.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() does not return a BouncyCastle provider
findings.body: The method `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is typically the SUN or SunJSSE provider, not BouncyCastle. Any caller relying on this method to obtain a BouncyCastle `Provider` instance (e.g., for algorithm lookups by provider name) will get incorrect behavior. Since this provider is meant for limited use, consider throwing `UnsupportedOperationException` like the other unsupported methods, or document clearly that this returns a fallback provider.

findings.title: Silent selection among multiple providers may mask misconfiguration
findings.body: Previously, having multiple `CryptoProvider` implementations on the classpath would throw an `IllegalStateException`, alerting users to a misconfiguration. Now the highest-order provider is silently selected and the rest are logged at DEBUG level. In production environments where DEBUG is typically disabled, a misconfiguration (e.g., accidentally including both FIPS and non-FIPS crypto jars) would go unnoticed, potentially leading to unexpected cryptographic behavior.
